lesson.title: Nonchord Tones
lesson.summary: Notes that do not belong to the chord decorate and connect the chord tones; how they are approached and left gives them their names.

section.title: Chord tones and nonchord tones
section.p: Melodies do not use only the notes of the chord that sounds with them. A nonchord tone, also called a non-harmonic tone or embellishing tone, is a note that does not belong to the current chord. It usually forms a dissonance with the chord and moves on to a chord tone.
Nonchord tones are named by three things:

list.li: How they are approached and left: by step, by leap, or by staying on the same note.
The direction: whether the melody continues in the same direction or turns back.
The metric position: unaccented, between the beats or on a weak beat, or accented, on a stronger beat than the note it resolves to.

check.prompt: What makes a note a nonchord tone?
check.option: It is not in the key
It does not belong to the chord sounding with it
It falls on a weak beat
check.explanation: A nonchord tone is defined against the current chord: most nonchord tones belong to the key but not to the chord. Many are unaccented, but suspensions and appoggiaturas fall on strong beats.

section.title: Passing and neighbour tones
section.p: A passing tone fills the gap between two chord tones a third apart: it is approached by step and left by step in the same direction. A neighbour tone decorates a single chord tone: it steps away, up or down, and steps back. Both are usually unaccented.

figure.caption: Over a C major chord: D5 is a passing tone between C5 and E5, and F5 an upper neighbour tone that returns to E5.

section.p: Passing tones can also fall on the beat, as accented passing tones, and two passing tones in a row can fill the gap of a fourth.

check.prompt: What kind of nonchord tone is the highlighted note?

figure.description: The bass staff holds a chord for the whole bar. Above it, three notes rise by step; the middle one, on the second beat, is highlighted.

check.explanation: Over the C major chord, F5 is not a chord tone. It is approached by step from E5 and left by step to G5, in the same direction, on a weak beat: a passing tone. A neighbour tone would return to E5.

section.title: Suspensions
section.p: A suspension holds a note over from one chord into the next, where it no longer fits, and then resolves it down by step. It has three parts:

list.li: The preparation: the note is a chord tone of the first chord.
The suspension: the same note, held or repeated, on a strong beat of the next chord, where it is a dissonance.
The resolution: the note falls a step to a chord tone.

figure.caption: A 4–3 suspension in C major. C5 is prepared over I, held into V on the third beat, where it is a fourth above the bass G, and resolves down to B4, the third.

section.p: Suspensions are named by the intervals above the bass at the suspension and the resolution: 4–3, 7–6 and 9–8 in an upper voice, and 2–3 when the bass itself is suspended. A suspension that resolves upward is called a retardation. While a suspension sounds, its note of resolution should not sound in another voice, except for the bass in a 9–8 suspension.

check.prompt: How does a suspension normally resolve?
check.explanation: The suspended note falls a step to a chord tone, as in 4–3 or 7–6. A suspension that rises instead is called a retardation.

check.prompt: In a 4–3 suspension, what do the numbers mean?
check.option: The suspension lasts four beats and the resolution three
A fourth above the bass resolves to a third above the bass
Degree 4 of the key resolves to degree 3
check.explanation: Like figures, the numbers count intervals above the bass: the suspended note is a fourth above it and resolves down to the third. In V of C major, the fourth above G is C and the third is B.

section.title: Appoggiaturas, escape tones and anticipations
section.p: Three more nonchord tones combine a step and a leap, or arrive early:

list.li: Appoggiatura: approached by leap and resolved by step, usually in the opposite direction. It is typically accented and expressive.
Escape tone: approached by step and left by leap in the opposite direction. It is unaccented.
Anticipation: a note of the next chord sounded early, before the chord arrives. It usually stays on the same note when the chord changes, and is common at cadences.

figure.caption: An appoggiatura in C major: the melody leaps up to F5 on the downbeat of I and resolves down by step to E5.
V–I in C major twice. First an escape tone: E5 steps up from D5 and leaps down to C5. Then an anticipation: C5 sounds over V, just before I arrives.

check.prompt: An accented nonchord tone is approached by leap and resolved by step in the opposite direction. What is it?
check.explanation: Leap in, step out, typically accented: an appoggiatura. An escape tone does the opposite, step in and leap out, and a passing tone moves by step on both sides.

section.title: Pedal point
section.p: A pedal point is a note held, usually in the bass, while the harmonies above it change, including chords that do not contain it. Tonic and dominant pedals are the most common: a tonic pedal often closes a piece, and a dominant pedal builds tension before the return of the tonic. A pedal in an upper voice is called an inverted pedal.

figure.caption: A tonic pedal in C major: I, IV, V7 and I over a held C3. Against V7 the pedal is a dissonance.

check.option: A note held while the chords above it change
A chord held while the bass moves
A note repeated on every beat by the soprano
check.explanation: A pedal point is a sustained note, usually in the bass, that continues while the harmonies change above it, even through chords that do not contain it.
